ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly medium-to-long turns: brief, informal check-ins and technical setup at the start give way to extended presentation monologues and multi-part audience questions. Overlap and interruptions are light but natural, with quick acknowledgments, greetings, and occasional self-corrections; speakers often jump in with “yeah,” “okay,” or “right” rather than waiting for highly formal handoffs. The tone is collegial and academically professional but relaxed, with abundant hedging (“I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “I guess,” “we’re interested in”), false starts, repeated words, and conversational fillers (“um,” “you know,” “like”). Participants build on one another by praising the work first, then framing questions as curiosity or extensions rather than challenges; disagreement is indirect and usually expressed as uncertainty, caveat, or an alternative interpretation. Questions tend to be long, exploratory, and multi-clause, often containing background reasoning before the actual question, while answers are similarly expansive, openly acknowledging limits and future directions.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether a nurse-led walk-in diabetes clinic at a safety-net hospital is working and for whom.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Patel
speakers.background: An internal medicine physician completing a PhD in clinical epidemiology, with seven years of safety-net hospital practice and prior work evaluating diabetes quality-improvement programs using electronic health record data. She is experienced with HbA1c trajectories, medication intensification, missed-appointment patterns, follow-up completion, and pragmatic comparison-group design.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya treats the clinic as a clinical service whose value must be assessed through feasible patient-level outcomes and care-process measures. She will prioritize defining an eligible patient cohort, measuring repeat HbA1c where available, no-show and follow-up rates, and relevant hospital quality indicators. She is careful about selection bias: HbA1c change can only be assessed among patients with repeat testing, and any comparison group requires agreed index dates, eligibility rules, and reliable data access.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Herrera
speakers.background: A medical sociologist and qualitative research engineer with nine years of experience designing interview, observation, and workflow-mapping studies in emergency departments, primary care clinics, and community health settings. His work examines institutional culture, professional boundary-making, stigma, and how patients navigate fragmented care under time and resource constraints.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Luis is concerned that visit counts and laboratory trends alone cannot explain who is able to use an evening and Saturday clinic or what kind of care patients actually encounter once there. He will focus on why patients seek care at unusual hours, how waiting, triage, language, stigma, and staff role arrangements shape experiences, and whether the clinic feels accessible or surveilling. He will press for ethics review and a recruitment process that does not interrupt care or make patients feel pressured to participate.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Okafor
speakers.background: A public health services researcher with fourteen years of experience leading evaluations of access initiatives in urban safety-net systems. She combines administrative-data analysis, community health assessment, implementation planning, and budget-impact work, with particular attention to racialized inequities, insurance instability, language access, and neighborhood-level barriers to chronic disease care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Aisha frames success as equitable reach and practical sustainability, not simply average improvement among people who attend. She will examine which populations the clinic reaches or misses relative to local diabetes burden, define the relevant catchment area and demographic groups, and assess funding, staffing, and expansion implications. She will coordinate a time-limited integrated design in which utilization and outcome patterns guide qualitative inquiry, while qualitative findings help interpret—not replace—quantitative results.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

meeting_opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting planning research next steps with 2-4 disciplines represented. The evaluated AI must map tasks to disciplines consistently with the discussion.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting planning research next steps with 2-4 disciplines represented. The evaluated AI must map tasks to disciplines consistently with the discussion.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Conduct a planning meeting among one clinical medicine representative, one sociology representative, and one public health representative. The meeting must produce coordinated next steps for a first-phase evaluation, with named discipline ownership and dependencies. Clinical medicine should explain that it can lead analysis of HbA1c change, comparison-group construction where feasible, no-show and follow-up rates, and relevant hospital quality metrics; it should note that HbA1c is only available for patients with repeat testing and that comparison groups need agreed eligibility dates and data access. Sociology should lead development of qualitative work on why patients use the clinic at odd hours, how clinic culture and staff roles shape care, stigma, and patients' experiences of waiting and being seen; it should state that interview and observation work requires ethics review and coordination so recruitment does not disrupt care. Public health should lead assessment of which populations the clinic reaches or misses, local diabetes burden, and funding and staffing implications; it should note that reach analyses depend on agreed catchment-area and demographic definitions and on clinical data extracts. The group should agree on an integrated design in which quantitative utilization and outcome findings identify patterns that qualitative work helps interpret, rather than treating one discipline's evidence as a replacement for another. They should assign a shared task to define the clinic's target population, core outcomes, and common eligibility period before analyses begin. They should also assign a joint data-governance/ethics step, including de-identification, approvals, and an interview recruitment process. Keep the discussion practical for the four-month funding deadline. Do not claim results or resolve questions that require data collection.

ground_truth.agreed_evaluation_approach: Use a mixed-methods first-phase evaluation. Clinical and public-health analyses will describe outcomes, use, follow-up, and reach; sociology will investigate mechanisms and patient/staff experience that explain observed patterns. Findings will be integrated after preliminary quantitative patterns are available.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: I was looking at the six-month sign-in summary, and the Saturday ZIP-code pattern is pretty striking, though it may just be small numbers. Before we get too far into methods, I'd like us today to get rough agreement on who counts as the population this clinic is meant to serve, and what we can realistically, um, learn before the funding decision. Then we can look at what the records actually support instead of building a very elegant plan around fields we don't have.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I think that has to come first, because the clinical outcomes depend on it. For a first pass, are we talking about adults with documented diabetes who used the walk-in clinic, or also people who came in with high glucose but no established diagnosis? And then we need the same eligibility period and an index date, probably the first walk-in visit, before I can tell whether enough people even have HbA1c results before and after.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: I'd keep both, but not collapse them. For the outcome work, we could define a core cohort of adults with documented diabetes. Then have a separate descriptive group for high-glucose or possible new-diagnosis visits, because excluding them makes the reach picture a little artificial. And for reach, we should decide if the denominator is hospital patients with diabetes or residents with diabetes in some agreed catchment. Those answer pretty different questions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: For the clinical piece, I’d make the hospital-patient-with-diabetes denominator the primary one, because we can actually identify it and ask whether this changed access or follow-up for people already in our care. A geographic denominator could sit alongside it for reach, but I’d worry about calling the clinic ineffective if people come from outside the usual catchment. Aisha, what local denominator could we get quickly enough that isn’t mostly, um, modeled estimates?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: I'd need to check the local health department's small-area estimates and see if they line up with ZIP codes or, better, the hospital's usual service-area geography. They're modeled, though, so I wouldn't use them as a precise denominator. We could show a simple secondary map of where users live against burden and maybe transit access, while keeping the hospital diabetes panel as the defensible primary denominator. The bigger question is whether we can get residential geography- whether we can get it cleanly enough from the EHR, even at an aggregated level.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: I’d be careful not to let the residence field stand in for access, though. In this population, an address can be unstable, shared, or just where mail goes. And ZIP-level patterns can look like preference when they’re really about insurance, transit, work schedules, or mobility. Could we make the map explicitly descriptive, then later ask people how they actually got here and what made these hours usable or not?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly, descriptive, and I’d probably suppress or combine very small areas rather than pretend the ZIP map is more stable than it is. Luis, for the interviews, what would you need to distinguish “the hours worked for me” from “I only came because someone in primary care sent me,” or from people who never knew it existed? That seems important for interpreting the Saturday concentration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: I think I’d want to separate referral pathway, awareness, and constraint, rather than treat them as competing explanations. In a brief post-care interview, we could ask how they first heard about it, why this particular visit happened now, what other option they considered, and whether the evening or Saturday slot changed the, um, the cost of coming, like missed work, childcare, transit, all that. But the people who never knew it existed are harder. Could the records tell us which eligible panel patients were ever offered or messaged about the clinic?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Maybe, but I wouldn’t assume the outreach fields are reliable until we inventory them. Portal messages, referral orders, after-visit instructions, any call logs, they may live in different places. In the first two weeks, if we can settle the eligibility and pull a small data dictionary, we could see whether there’s even a usable “offered or referred” marker. Otherwise, the non-user question needs a different, different sampling route.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Before we use referral or outreach as an exposure, I’d want to know if it was recorded consistently across settings. I’m seeing a related issue in the preliminary charts. Some people had a follow-up booked after medication review, but there’s no completed visit in our scheduling extract. Do we know if outside visits or cancellations show up anywhere, so we could tell those apart from a true no-show?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: That distinction matters a lot because “missed follow-up” can become a moralized proxy for disengagement when it may be an outside encounter or a scheduling artifact. Maya, does the extract have- do we know if it has cancellation reasons, reschedule attempts, or any linkage to outside claims at all, or are we really just seeing absence from our own scheduling system?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: At the moment, I honestly don't know. The preliminary pull was basically our scheduling and encounter data, so an absent completion could be a no-show, a cancellation, care elsewhere, or just a linkage issue- a linkage problem. I don't think outside claims are in scope, but I need to verify that with data services. I'd label it more cautiously as documented follow-up completion, and maybe separately inspect cancellation and rescheduling fields if they exist.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: That cautious label should carry into the interview sampling too. If we recruit people just because the record marks them as a no-show, we may be selecting a documentation category rather than a shared care experience. Could we- could we wait for that field audit, then sample across completed, cancelled, and unresolved follow-up statuses?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, yeah, that feels important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: For the quantitative side, I’d resist making no-show a core outcome until we know those statuses are real. We can still look at whether a follow-up was scheduled, then report documented completion, cancellation or rescheduling, and unresolved records separately. That audit also tells Luis what the interview strata actually mean.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Yeah, I’d want to see that audit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Given the four-month clock, weeks one and two need to be the field audit and the shared definitions. Eligibility, first walk-in as index, geography, and what each follow-up status actually means. Then the early descriptive patterns can- we can let those drive the interview strata, instead of locking Luis into categories that don't actually exist in the data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: That sequence works for me. I’d add that the field audit needs to check whether sign-in records can actually link to the EHR, labs, and scheduling through a stable patient identifier. Otherwise, even using the first walk-in as the index date gets slippery. Once we know that, I can quickly count how many core-cohort patients have an HbA1c on either side of that date, instead of promising a change analysis we can’t support.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: And that linkage check is also the gate for the reach work. If the sign-in file only partly links, our hospital-panel denominator could be biased in ways we won't see. Maybe weeks three through six are just extraction and basic linkage and descriptives, including use by evening versus Saturday and the panel comparison, while Maya checks the lab windows. Then we decide what the data can bear before treating any pattern as a gap.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: That seems like the right gate. For the panel comparison, though, I'd keep it descriptive at first, walk-in users versus otherwise eligible diabetes-panel patients, because people who choose or are directed to walk in may be pretty different clinically and in their access needs. After the linkage audit, we can see whether there's enough baseline information to make any adjusted comparison defensible, but I wouldn't build the funding decision around it yet...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: And if adjustment isn’t supportable, that’s still useful for leadership. We can say what the clinic is reaching without implying causation. Then maybe weeks seven through eleven are the preliminary pattern review, plus interviews and a first look at staffing schedules and cost inputs. I need to see whether those records are complete, complete enough before we call anything a sustainability estimate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: One caution on putting interviews in weeks seven through eleven, ethics review and the clinic's recruitment workflow need to start alongside the field audit. Even if sampling waits for the patterns, I need to check whether brief post-care contact is permissible and find a point that is after triage and doesn't make someone feel their care depends on saying yes. Otherwise we may have the data strata- we may have the data strata but no ethically workable way to reach people in time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: Those approvals and the recruitment workflow need to run in parallel, not after the quantitative pull. And it would help if the interview protocol can ask about whether people got follow-up elsewhere, because that may be the only way we can interpret some of those unresolved scheduling records without- without overstating them.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: Let’s start the ethics and recruitment piece now, and leave the sampling details provisional until the audit. Then weeks twelve through sixteen can be the integration window, where we look at what the utilization, follow-up, interviews, and whatever staffing-cost data we have actually say together, so we’re not trying to put the funding brief together at the last—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Patel
transcript.text: I think we've covered what we needed to cover today. Let's pick this up once the field audit and approvals are moving. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Okafor
transcript.text: All right, take care, everybody.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Herrera
transcript.text: Thanks, bye.
